conditions: The target item is a spreadsheet (a file of spreadsheet type, e.g. .xlsx/.csv/Box spreadsheet).
Priya Nair (a specific, identifiable user) has left a comment on that file in Box.
The subject matter — either the spreadsheet's content or the comment itself, see ambiguity — concerns travel costs.
There is exactly one such spreadsheet meeting the above criteria (the request assumes a unique match).
The action to perform is adding the tag "travel-reviewed" to that file.

ambiguities.phrase: the spreadsheet ... commented on about travel costs
readings: "about travel costs" describes the spreadsheet itself (a spreadsheet whose subject/content is travel costs), and Priya Nair's comment could be about anything
"about travel costs" describes the content of Priya Nair's comment (the comment text discusses travel costs), regardless of whether the spreadsheet's overall subject is travel
Left a comment through Box's native comment feature on the file
More loosely, made any remark associated with the file (e.g. in a task or annotation), though this is a stretch

records.note: Q3 forecast.xlsx has a comment from Priya Nair (30000000006) explicitly asking to double-check the travel costs in the forecast — this satisfies the reading where 'about travel costs' describes the comment's content, and it is the only file with a comment that is actually about travel costs, so r4 (uniqueness) holds too. It is contestable because under the alternate reading ('about travel costs' modifying 'spreadsheet'), a colleague could argue this file isn't itself a travel-costs document, just a general Q3 forecast that mentions travel costs as one line item, so r3 could be said to fail on that reading.

Travel costs 2026.xlsx is named for travel costs, but the comment from Priya Nair on it is 'Please add the hiring plan numbers' — unrelated to travel costs. Under the reading where 'about travel costs' describes the comment's content (which I judge more natural, since the phrase sits immediately after 'commented on'), this fails r3. It is contestable because a colleague reading 'about travel costs' as describing the spreadsheet itself would pick this file on its title alone — a classic name-matches-but-comment-doesn't near miss.

turn2.differences: The author's conditions match my own step-1 conditions exactly, including carrying forward the scope ambiguity of 'about travel costs' into r3 rather than resolving it. No substantive differences.

ambiguity_effects.explain: Could mean the spreadsheet's own subject matter is travel costs (favoring 3102, 'Travel costs 2026.xlsx'), or that Priya Nair's comment itself is about travel costs (favoring 3101, whose comment reads 'double-check the travel costs in this forecast'). The two readings pick different, mutually exclusive files, and the sentence structure ('commented on about travel costs') does not cleanly disambiguate which noun/verb it modifies, though the immediate adjacency to 'commented on' gives a slight edge to the comment-content reading.
In this dataset the only comment-like records are standard Box file comments, so there is no practical alternative reading (e.g. tasks or annotations) that would change which file is selected.

turn2.naturalness_note: Reads like a plausible real workplace request (tagging a reviewed expense-related spreadsheet after a colleague's comment); no artificial or test-only phrasing.
